vignette:
She is 45 now, a single European woman who has spent most of her adult life in military aviation, and she still speaks about herself first as a pilot. For years, flying has been the one place where her mind feels ordered and her body knows exactly what to do. The traumatic event interrupts that certainty in an instant. While on deployment, she is part of an air mission over a region where a civilian target has been struck by a terrorist attack. The assignment is already tense, but what stays with her is not the technical side of the flight. It is the moment she sees the aftermath on the ground: smoke rising, broken structures, bodies moving in confusion, the sudden understanding that this is not an abstract threat but human devastation unfolding below her. She is trained to keep distance, to follow procedure, to speak in measured terms over the radio. Instead, she feels a sharp, almost physical collapse inside herself as the scale of the violence becomes clear.

In the days that follow, she does what she has always done when under pressure: she works. She checks equipment, flies the next mission, answers questions in short, efficient sentences. She tells herself that being functional means she is coping. Yet even then, she notices that the image of the attack returns without invitation, most often when she is trying to focus on routine tasks. She sees smoke where there is none, hears fragments of radio chatter in her head, and catches herself replaying the sequence of events with a kind of rigid scrutiny, as if finding the correct detail might make the memory settle into place. Sleep becomes lighter and less restorative. She wakes with her heart pounding, already braced for something terrible, and lies awake listening to ordinary sounds in the dark.

As time goes on, she becomes more vigilant in ways that others interpret as professionalism. She scans rooms automatically. She prefers to sit where she can see exits. In public places, she notices entrances, crowds, and sudden noises with a sharpness that leaves her exhausted. The smell of fuel, burning materials, or even a sharp chemical odor can pull her abruptly back to the attack site, and she feels the same tightening in her chest that she felt that day. She tries to ignore it, but the body remembers before the mind can argue. At times she is irritated by small things that never used to bother her. A dropped tray in a cafeteria, a helicopter overhead, a loud door slamming — each can cause a surge of anger or a jolt that she then hides immediately. She dislikes being seen as rattled, so she becomes even more controlled on the outside, which costs her a great deal of energy.

She also begins to pull away from people. She has never been especially dependent on others, but now conversations feel effortful and often pointless. Colleagues say she seems distant. She keeps relationships superficial because closeness requires a kind of openness she cannot manage. Being single has not bothered her in the past, yet now it also reflects how little space she feels she has for anyone else’s needs or questions. She does not want to explain why she has gone quiet or why she is avoiding certain news broadcasts, certain anniversaries, certain streets in the city that remind her of the mission. She notices that she no longer allows herself to feel much when she sees stories of civilian casualties or attacks on television. She can become detached, almost numb, and then unexpectedly overwhelmed by shame that she is still alive and functioning while others died in the attack she witnessed from above.

Her work as a combat pilot remains central, but it also becomes complicated. She can still perform, and in some ways she performs better because she is trying so hard to prove nothing has changed. At the same time, she has moments of hesitation before takeoff, brief spells of disorientation in the cockpit, and a growing dread that she might lose focus at the wrong moment. She begins to overcheck everything. Small mistakes by others trigger disproportionate anger in her, followed by self-reproach. She has less patience, less ease, and less trust in her own body. The discipline that once felt like strength now sometimes feels like a tight shell holding everything in.

By the time she comes to therapy, she has been living this way for a long time. She is articulate and composed, but there is strain in the way she holds herself, as though she is still bracing for impact. She says she is used to being the one who stays calm in a crisis, yet she now recognizes that her life has narrowed around avoiding reminders and staying in control. Even so, she continues to show up, to fly, to carry responsibility, and to move through each day with the same determination that has always defined her.
